title: Separation of Powers — Montesquieu and Classical Formulation

content.overview: Montesquieu's classical account in The Spirit of the Laws linked political liberty to the separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers. His formulation influenced constitutional design worldwide, though practical systems vary in rigidity.
content.glance: State Montesquieu's three-fold division and its liberty rationale; contrast with the Indian checks-and-balances model; avoid treating Montesquieu as a rigid code for India.
content.study: Montesquieu argued that liberty is endangered when the same body makes, executes and adjudicates law. His theory shaped constitutional thought but was not adopted in pure form anywhere. Parliamentary systems fuse legislature and executive to a degree; the US model is more separated. India blends separation with accountability of the executive to the legislature and strong judicial review. Current-law framing: cite Montesquieu as theory; apply Indian constitutional text and cases for doctrine. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

examples.title: Theory versus positive law
examples.body: An answer that cites only Montesquieu without Indian authorities is incomplete. Theory explains origin; Indian cases supply doctrine.

examples.title: Parliamentary fusion
examples.body: Responsible government draws the executive from the legislature. This is a permitted design choice, not a Montesquieu violation under Indian law.

hypotheticals.question: Is Montesquieu binding Indian precedent?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. He is a political theorist; Indian law is the Constitution and cases.

hypotheticals.question: Does any fusion of powers violate Montesquieu and void the measure in India?
hypotheticals.analysis: Indian parliamentary government involves responsible fusion within constitutional limits.

cases.name: Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab
cases.facts: Executive action and constitutional distribution of governmental functions.
cases.issue: Whether the Indian Constitution adopts a rigid separation of powers.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Constitution does not impose separation in absolute rigidity.
cases.holding: Functional separation rather than strict Montesquieuan separation recognised.
cases.relevance: Principal Indian authority contrasting classical and Indian separation.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.issue: Whether separation of powers forms part of the constitutional structure.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Checks and balances and separation of powers are components of the basic structure.

cases.name: Asif Hameed v State of Jammu and Kashmir
cases.facts: Limits of judicial intervention in matters allocated to other organs.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Each constitutional organ must operate within its assigned sphere.
